meta.title: Who really said "There is a Conspiracy of Silence Against Me. What Should I Do, Oscar? Join It"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Oscar Wilde coined “join it” — but he said it to Augustine Birrell, not to the poet’s face. The 1893 diary and 1916 memoir that show it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is a Conspiracy of Silence Against Me. What Should I Do, Oscar? Join It'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilde’s cruellest advice was never delivered in person. Birrell asked him what he should have said — and Wilde told him.

answer.label: Not Augustine Birrell — the retort is Oscar Wilde’s
answer.sourceLine: Wilde made the joke, but not to the poet who prompted it. A neglected poet complained to the Liberal politician Augustine Birrell that there was a conspiracy of silence against his book; Birrell, stuck for a reply, put the problem to Wilde, who told him what he should have said. Birrell was telling the story at a dinner party on 19 April 1893, and it reached print in the face-to-face form people now repeat by October 1894.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Robert Harborough Sherard, 1916, pp. 300–302, quoting Augustine Birrell
Sir Algernon West’s diary, 19 April 1893 — published 1922
The Critic, 13 October 1894, p. 240 — the face-to-face version, poet unnamed

source.excerpt: “That reminds me of a certain poet who came to me once upon a time and complained that his works were neglected. He said there was a conspiracy of silence. Of course I felt very sorry for him, but I was really puzzled what to say. I mentioned this to a well-known wit, who exclaimed quite angrily: ‘You did not know what to say! Do you really mean to tell me that you did not know what to say?’ ‘No, upon my word I did not.’ ‘Of course, you should have said: “A conspiracy of silence! My dear fellow, join it at once.”’”
trail: 19 April 1893 — the earliest dated telling, and it is Birrell’s. Sir Algernon West’s diary records a dinner at Asquith’s where the table “discussed whether Oscar Wilde was really witty; Birrell contended he was, and gave this instance: He had met L. Morris, who said, ‘I have written a book, and not a paper nor a review has alluded to it. There is a conspiracy of silence.’ ‘Directly after, I met Oscar Wilde and asked him what I ought to have said. “You should have said,” answered Oscar Wilde: “My dear Morris, join it yourself.”’” Chapter X of the diary is headed 1893. Private Diaries of Sir Algernon West, p. 134 ↗

13 October 1894 — the story reaches print in The Critic, credited to The Bookman, already in the form people repeat: the poet asks Wilde directly and Wilde answers “Join it.” The poet is left nameless. Quote Investigator, which reproduces the passage ↗

1916 — Sherard prints Birrell’s own account and says plainly why he doubts the face-to-face version: “I never believed that Oscar Wilde would have said such a thing to a brother poet, because I never knew him wilfully to hurt anybody’s feelings.” The Real Oscar Wilde, pp. 300–302 ↗
The verdict — Quote Investigator concludes that Wilde “crafted this witty chastisement, but did not mock Lewis Morris directly,” finding Sherard’s and West’s testimony plausible. Quote Investigator ↗
source.excerptNote: Birrell does not name the wit in this account. Sherard, printing it, identifies him as Wilde and adds — “Oscar seems here to have been quick in repartee” — and in Algernon West’s diary entry Birrell names Wilde outright.

Wilde himself died in 1900. The wording quoted here is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: About Oscar Wilde
author.bio: Oscar Wilde was an Irish poet, playwright and critic, and by the early 1890s one of the most popular and influential dramatists in London. A Woman of No Importance — the play West’s wife had been to see on the night this story was told — was first given at the Haymarket Theatre that very day, 19 April 1893. Wilde’s reputation as an instant wit is partly a construction: his friend Robert Sherard, who knew him well, thought most of his best lines were “elaborated after the event,” and this anecdote is a good example of one polished in the retelling.

copyAttribution: "A conspiracy of silence! My dear fellow, join it at once." — Oscar Wilde, advising Augustine Birrell on the reply he should have given a neglected poet. Recorded in Robert Harborough Sherard, The Real Oscar Wilde (London: T. Werner Laurie, 1916), 300–302; told by Birrell at a dinner on 19 April 1893 and first printed, in the face-to-face form, in The Critic on 13 October 1894. Wilde did not say it to the poet directly.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The words are Wilde’s. Almost everything else about the way this story is told has moved — who was asked, who answered, and to whose face.

items.scope: The name on this page’s file
items.why: Quote Investigator lists Birrell among the candidate speakers, and he is the source of the best-evidenced account — but in that account he is explicitly the man who could not think of a reply: “I was really puzzled what to say.” The line came from the wit he consulted. Quote Investigator ↗

items.who: “What should I do, Oscar?” — the poet asking Wilde to his face
items.why: This is the 1894 newspaper form, and it is the one everyone repeats. Wilde’s own circle disputed it: Sherard thought Wilde never wilfully hurt anyone’s feelings, and that the poet was “insufficiently popular to excite anybody’s hostility.” The Real Oscar Wilde, p. 300 ↗

In 1907 Life ran the joke as the American playwright Clyde Fitch’s, told about an aspiring novelist. The anecdote was already thirteen years in print by then; Quote Investigator allows that Fitch may have used the punchline but not that he originated it. Quote Investigator ↗
Named by Birrell in 1893 and by later retellings, Morris was a popular Anglo-Welsh poet whose verse the reviewers ignored. He is the man complaining, never the man answering.

misattribution.truthLine: Wilde coined it; Birrell carried the complaint to him. Quote Investigator’s full chronology ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The setting of the earliest telling is almost better than the joke. The diary of Sir Algernon West records a dinner at Asquith’s on 19 April 1893 — Birrell, John Morley, the Lytteltons, J. Tennant — at which the table fell to arguing whether Oscar Wilde was really witty. Birrell said he was, and produced this story as his evidence.

That is the same day A Woman of No Importance was first given at the Haymarket Theatre in London, and West notes in the same entry that his wife had been to see it. Wilde’s reputation was the evening’s subject in more than one room.
detailsBody: The fuller version matters because it changes the joke’s cruelty. In the popular form Wilde tells a struggling poet, to his face, to help the world ignore him. In Birrell’s form Wilde is coaching a friend on the reply he wished he had made — still merciless about the poet, but delivered safely out of earshot.

Sherard, who knew Wilde, thought the distinction decisive, and printed Birrell’s account specifically to correct the record. His own comment on it is the shrewdest thing anyone has said about Wilde’s reputation as a talker: “I think that for the most part the good things he said were elaborated after the event.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Wilde crafted the retort but did not mock Lewis Morris directly; the earliest published report it located is The Critic of 13 October 1894 (credited to The Bookman, poet unnamed); Sherard 1916 pp. 300-302 prints Birrell’s account; the 1922 Private Diaries of Sir Algernon West record Birrell telling it with Wilde named; and in 1907 Life credited the punchline to Clyde Fitch.

Sherard, The Real Oscar Wilde (1916), pp. 300-302, prints Birrell’s statement verbatim: the poet complained of a conspiracy of silence, Birrell was "really puzzled what to say", and a "well-known wit" told him he should have said "A conspiracy of silence! My dear fellow, join it at once." Sherard adds that he never believed Wilde would have said such a thing to a brother poet.

The Private Diaries of Sir Algernon West (London: John Murray, 1922), p. 134, in Chapter X headed 1893, records the dinner at Asquith’s where it "was discussed whether Oscar Wilde was really witty; Birrell contended he was" and gave the L. Morris story, with Wilde answering "My dear Morris, join it yourself."
Oscar Wilde (16 October 1854 – 30 November 1900) was an Irish author, poet and playwright.
Augustine Birrell (19 January 1850 – 20 November 1933) was a British Liberal Party politician who was Chief Secretary for Ireland from 1907 to 1916.
Sir Lewis Morris (23 January 1833 – 12 November 1907) was a Welsh academic, politician and popular poet of the Anglo-Welsh school.
A Woman of No Importance by Oscar Wilde was first given on 19 April 1893 at the Haymarket Theatre, London.
